name: Quantum Key Distribution
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Key Exchange That Catches Its Own Eavesdropper
lesson.summary: Quantum key distribution uses single photons, not qubits performing computation, to let two parties share a secret key while detecting any eavesdropper, and it is already running in real government, financial, and telecom networks today, distinct from and years ahead of fault-tolerant quantum computing.
lesson.body:
Public key encryption, covered earlier, relies on mathematical problems, like factoring large numbers, that are hard for classical computers but would become easy for a large, fault-tolerant quantum computer running Shor's algorithm. That threat is real but distant, because building a quantum computer capable of running Shor's algorithm on real world key sizes requires the same million qubit scale, error corrected hardware discussed earlier, hardware that does not exist yet. Quantum key distribution, or QKD, is a completely different technology aimed at a related problem, and confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes in popular coverage of quantum security.

QKD does not use a quantum computer at all. It uses quantum sensing style physics, specifically the fact that measuring a quantum system generally disturbs it, to let two parties, conventionally named Alice and Bob, establish a shared secret key over a channel that reveals any eavesdropper. In the original and still most common protocol, BB84, published by Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard in 1984, Alice sends a stream of single photons, each encoded in one of two randomly chosen measurement bases. Because of the no cloning theorem and the disturbance caused by measurement in the wrong basis, an eavesdropper who intercepts and measures the photons to learn the key, then resends them, unavoidably introduces detectable errors into the fraction of the signal that Alice and Bob later compare openly. If the error rate is low enough, they know the channel was not compromised and can trust the remaining, unrevealed bits as a shared secret key.

This is not a future technology. China has operated a terrestrial QKD backbone connecting Beijing and Shanghai, spanning roughly two thousand kilometers, using trusted relay nodes to extend the range beyond what a single fiber link can achieve. China also launched the Micius satellite in 2016, which demonstrated satellite based QKD and quantum secured video calls between ground stations thousands of kilometers apart. Commercial QKD hardware from companies including ID Quantique and Toshiba has been deployed for point to point links protecting financial transactions and government communications in several countries, and Switzerland has used QKD protected links to transmit federal election results.

It is worth being precise about QKD's real limitations, because overselling it is as misleading as ignoring it. QKD generally requires either a dedicated fiber link or a satellite line of sight, does not by itself scale easily to the kind of any to any internet communication that public key encryption handles today, and still depends on classical authentication to prevent a man in the middle attack, which means it is not a total replacement for existing cryptographic infrastructure so much as a specialized hardening layer for specific high value links. There is also a genuine, unresolved debate in the security community about whether QKD is worth its cost and deployment complexity given the parallel development of post quantum cryptography, meaning classical algorithms redesigned to resist even a future quantum computer, which the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology finalized as formal standards in 2024. Reasonable experts disagree on how much of the QKD investment will look prescient in twenty years versus how much will look like an expensive detour, and this book will not pretend to settle that argument. What is not in dispute is that QKD is a real, working, already deployed application of quantum physics to security, built on quantum sensing style single photon physics rather than on the fault-tolerant quantum computing this book has spent so much time being skeptical of.
